facts.statement: The only known species of Noasaurus is Noasaurus leali.
facts.quote: The type and only species is N. leali.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Noasaurus measures between 1.6 and 2 meters in length.
facts.quote: Noasaurus was a fairly small theropod, with PVL 4061 measuring somewhere between 1.6–2 m in length.

facts.statement: Curved claws initially thought to be foot claws were later identified as belonging to the forelimbs, resembling those of spinosaurids.
facts.quote: Initially, it was believed that two strongly curved unguals (claws) found alongside the holotype were evidence of raptorial foot claws, like those of dromaeosaurids. However, it is now known that they belonged to Noasaurus' forelimbs, and were thus functionally similar to those of spinosaurids.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Noasaurus was an opportunistic mesopredator that likely fed on small vertebrates and fish.
facts.quote: Therefore, rather than converging on dromaeosaurids, it may have been an opportunistic mesopredator, feeding on small vertebrates, including fish.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen PVL 4061 was discovered in 1975 in the Lecho Formation of Southern Salta by a team led by José Fernando Bonaparte.
facts.quote: The fragmentary holotype specimen of Noasaurus, PVL 4061, consisting of a few cranial and postcranial bones, was discovered from strata from the Lecho Formation of Southern Salta in 1975 by a team led by José Fernando Bonaparte.

facts.statement: Noasaurus was originally described in 1980 as a coelurosaur and placed in its own family, Noasauridae, which is now classified within Ceratosauria.
facts.quote: When described by Bonaparte and in PhD student Jaime Powell in 1980, it was believed to be a coelurosaur theropod and assigned to a family of its own; this family, Noasauridae, still exists, though has been reassigned to Ceratosauria.

facts.statement: Noasaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 68 million years ago.
facts.quote: These layers derive from the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous Period, dating to between 70 million and 68 million years old.

facts.statement: Noasaurus leali was named and described by Bonaparte and Powell in 1980.
facts.quote: The type and only known species, Noasaurus leali, was named and briefly described by Bonaparte and Powell in 1980 alongside Saltasaurus.

facts.statement: The species name 'leali' honors Juan Carlos Leal, the discoverer of the fossil site.
facts.quote: The specific name honours the discoverer of the site, Juan Carlos Leal.

facts.statement: A 2024 study led by Christophe Hendrickx provided a detailed re-evaluation of the Noasaurus holotype.
facts.quote: In 2024, a study by an international team of researchers led by Christophe Hendrickx described the holotype of Noasaurus in further detail and evaluated its paleobiology, paleoecology, classification, and anatomy.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Noasaurus to be 1.5 meters long and weigh 15 kilograms.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 1.5 m and its weight at 15 kg.

facts.statement: A 2024 study estimated Noasaurus lengths of 1.6 meters and 2 meters based on skull and metatarsal dimensions.
facts.quote: In 2024, Hendrickx et al. used the reconstructed size of the skull and the dimensions of the second metatarsal to provide length estimates of 1.6 m and 2 m, respectively.

facts.statement: Researchers did not provide a weight estimate because the holotype lacked necessary limb elements and might have been a juvenile.
facts.quote: They abstained from providing a mass estimate due to the lack of the necessary limb elements, and the possibility that the Noasaurus holotype was a juvenile.

facts.statement: The skull anatomy of Noasaurus is poorly known because only a left maxilla and a right quadrate are preserved.
facts.quote: The general skull anatomy of Noasaurus is poorly known, as only two cranial elements are preserved: a left maxilla and a right quadrate, both fairly complete.

facts.statement: Noasaurus possessed ziphodont teeth that were laterally compressed, recurved, and serrated on both edges.
facts.quote: Its teeth were ziphodont: they were compressed laterally (from side-to-side), recurved, and bore fine serrations on the front and rear edges, as in many other theropods.

facts.statement: The preserved teeth of Noasaurus did not exceed 10 millimeters in height.
facts.quote: None of the preserved crowns appear to have exceeded 10 mm in height.

facts.statement: Noasaurus likely had a long, S-shaped neck based on comparisons with related dinosaurs and the elongation of its known neck bones.
facts.quote: Based on comparisons with other noasaurids and the overall elongation of the known cervical elements, it is likely that Noasaurus' neck was long and sigmoidal, meaning it bore a strong S-shaped curve.

facts.statement: Two claw-bearing finger bones were found with the main skeleton of Noasaurus.
facts.quote: Two unguals, phalanges which in life would have supported keratinous claws, were found in association with Noasaurus holotype.

facts.statement: Studies showed that the large, curved claws originally thought to be on Noasaurus's feet actually belonged to its hands.
facts.quote: While initially believed to be raptorial foot claws, similar to those of the unrelated dromaeosaurids, subsequent studies have demonstrated that the claws instead came from the manus (hand).

facts.statement: The only known bone from Noasaurus's hind leg is the second metatarsal.
facts.quote: The only known hind limb element is the second right metatarsal.

facts.statement: A bulge on the known hind leg bone likely served as an attachment point for muscles that extended the second toe.
facts.quote: The medial surface bears a low, elliptical bulge, likely serving as a muscle attachment point, and as the point of origin for the extensor muscles of the second digit.

facts.statement: Bony projections on the sides of Noasaurus's neck vertebrae were expanded and covered most of the bone's length.
facts.quote: The epipophyses, bony projections on the sides of the cervical vertebrae, are expanded and occupy most of the arch's length.

facts.statement: Noasaurus was a small theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: Noasaurus era un pequeño terópodo.

facts.statement: Noasaurus had at least eleven teeth in its upper jaw.
facts.quote: El maxilar tiene al menos once dientes.

facts.statement: Noasaurus's teeth were curved backward and had ridges on their front and back edges.
facts.quote: Los dientes son recurvados y tienen estrías en los bordes delantero y trasero.

facts.statement: It was originally believed that Noasaurus had a retractable claw similar to that of dromaeosaurs, but through independent evolution.
facts.quote: Originalmente se creyó que poseía una garra retráctil similar a la de los dromeosáuridos pero de evolución independiente.

facts.statement: Later studies showed that the claw actually came from the hand.
facts.quote: Estudios posteriores mostraron que la garra en realidad provenía de la mano.

facts.statement: The claw was exceptionally curved, had parallel base sides in top view, and possessed a deep triangular cavity at the bottom of the base.
facts.quote: a garra es excepcionalmente curva, tiene lados de base paralelos en la vista superior y posee una cavidad triangular profunda en la parte inferior de la base.

facts.statement: Noasaurus was described as a fossil taxon in 1980.
facts.quote: Category:Fossil taxa described in 1980

facts.statement: The name Noasaurus was coined by José Bonaparte.
facts.quote: Category:Taxa named by José Bonaparte

facts.statement: The name Noasaurus was also coined by Jaime Powell.
facts.quote: Category:Taxa named by Jaime Powell

facts.statement: Noasaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 70 million years ago between the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages, in what is now South America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 70 millones de años, entre el Campaniaense y el Maastrichtiense, en lo que hoy es Sudamérica.

facts.statement: The environment where Noasaurus lived was a coastal plain with ponds and lagoons that likely supported a tropical coastal forest.
facts.quote: The stratigraphic composition of the Lecho Formation, from which the holotype of Noasaurus is known, suggests that its depositional environment was a coastal plain, pockmarked with ponds and lagoons, which likely supported a tropical coastal forest.

facts.statement: Noasaurus lived in a hot, humid environment likely near the Tropic of Capricorn.
facts.quote: It was a hot, humid environment, likely close to the Tropic of Capricorn.

facts.statement: Noasaurus is currently classified as a member of the Ceratosauria.
facts.quote: Classification Noasaurus is today considered to be a member of the Ceratosauria.

facts.statement: Bonaparte and Powell originally assigned Noasaurus to its own family, the Noasauridae.
facts.quote: Bonaparte and Powell assigned it to a family of its own, the Noasauridae.

facts.statement: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul classified Noasauridae as a subfamily within Abelisauridae.
facts.quote: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul subsumed Noasauridae into Abelisauridae as a subfamily.

facts.statement: Modern analyses show that noasaurids form their own clade, Abelisauroidea, within Ceratosauria, closely related to abelisaurids.
facts.quote: While subsequent analyses have consistently recovered noasaurids as close relatives of abelisaurids, starting with a 1991 paper by José Bonaparte, they now form a clade of their own, Abelisauroidea, within Ceratosauria.

facts.statement: The genus Noasaurus was established by Bonaparte and Powell in 1980.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Bonaparte & Powell, 1980

facts.statement: The species Noasaurus leali was named by Bonaparte and Powell in 1980.
facts.quote: species_authority: Bonaparte & Powell, 1980

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the hand claw may have been used to catch fish, a trait convergent with spinosaurids like Baryonyx.
facts.quote: Instead, as proposed by Hendrickx et al.. in 2024, it may have been utilised to snag fish from the water, making it instead convergent with the enlarged thumb claw of spinosaurids like Baryonyx.

facts.statement: Noasaurus was likely an opportunistic mid-sized predator that fed on small vertebrates like fish.
facts.quote: They concluded that it was likely an opportunistic mesopredator that fed on small vertebrates, such as fishes.

facts.statement: There was a debate over whether the large curved claws belonged to the feet or hands, with later studies confirming they were hand claws.
facts.quote: While initially believed to be raptorial foot claws, similar to those of the unrelated dromaeosaurids, subsequent studies have demonstrated that the claws instead came from the manus (hand).

facts.statement: In 1988, Paul hypothesized that noasaurines were South American counterparts of dromaeosaurids through convergent evolution, a view later undermined by the discovery that the claws were on the hands.
facts.quote: Paul in 1988 saw the noasaurines as the South-American counterparts of the Asian and North-American dromaeosaurids, in a process of convergent evolution.

facts.statement: Paul hypothesized that Noasaurus might have used a kicking technique to disembowel prey due to short forelimbs, assuming it used foot claws like dromaeosaurids, but this was disproven when the claws were identified as hand claws.
facts.quote: Noting that abelisaurids tend to have very short arms, he wondered whether the forelimbs of Noasaurus were of limited length also, forcing the animal to employ a kicking technique instead of grasping the back of a victim in order to disembowel it with the foot claws, a method he assumed the dromaeosaurids used.

facts.statement: In 2024, Hendrickx et al. placed Noasaurus in a polytomy with other small noasaurids, suggesting a radiation of small-bodied forms during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: In 2024, Hendrickx et al.. recovered Noasaurus in a polytomy with Laevisuchus, Masiakasaurus, Velocisaurus, and Vespersaurus, likely representing a radiation of small-bodied noasaurids that occurred during the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The species Noasaurus leali was formally described in 1980.
facts.quote: La especie tipo, Noasaurus leali, fue descrita en 1980.

facts.statement: Fossils of Noasaurus come from the El Lecho Formation at El Brete in Salta Province, northeastern Argentina.
facts.quote: Los fósiles provienen de la Formación El Lecho, en El Brete, Provincia de Salta, en el noreste de la Argentina.

facts.statement: The discovery was first reported in scientific literature in 1977.
facts.quote: En 1977, el descubrimiento se informó en la literatura científica.

facts.statement: The specific name 'leali' honors the site owner, Fidel Leal.
facts.quote: El nombre específico honra al propietario del sitio, Fidel Leal.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen PVL 4061 dates to the early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 million years ago.
facts.quote: El holotipo, PVL 4061, se encontró en una capa de la Formación Lecho de la provincia de Salta, Argentina, que data del período Cretácico tardío, más precisamente la etapa temprana de Maastrichtiense, hace aproximadamente 70 millones de años.

facts.statement: In 2004, one of the hand claws was re-identified as belonging to the hand rather than the foot.
facts.quote: En 2004, se reconoció como una garra de mano, en cuyo caso se remitió la garra de segunda mano.

facts.statement: A cervical vertebra found at the site was initially identified in 1999 as oviraptorosaurian, suggesting a rare presence of that group in Gondwana.
facts.quote: En 1999, una vértebra cervical encontrada en el sitio, el espécimen MACM 622, fue identificada como oviraptorosauriano, una prueba rara de que la Oviraptorosauria había invadido los continentes de Gondwana.

facts.statement: In 2007, that same vertebra was re-identified as belonging to Noasaurus.
facts.quote: En 2007, sin embargo, fue reidentificado como una vértebra noasáurida, probablemente perteneciente al holotipo Noasaurus.

facts.statement: In April 1975, an expedition led by Professor José F. Bonaparte set out to find fossils in the El Brete area of Salta Province.
facts.quote: Durante abril de 1975, un equipo de la Fundación Miguel Lillo, de San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina, dirigido por el profesor José F. Bonaparte, emprendió una expedición a la región sur de la provincia de Salta con el objetivo de localizar nuevos restos fósiles en la zona conocida como El Brete.

facts.statement: Juan Carlos Leal discovered a particularly rich fossil site on a small hill at Estancia El Brete.
facts.quote: Este último fue quien descubrió, en una pequeña colina de la Estancia El Brete, un yacimiento particularmente rico en fósiles.

facts.statement: Recovered materials included remains of at least five sauropod individuals, including the titanosaur Saltasaurus loricatus.
facts.quote: Entre los materiales recuperados, además del pequeño celurosaurio Noasaurus leali, se identificaron restos pertenecientes a al menos cinco individuos de saurópodos, entre ellos el titanosaurio Saltasaurus loricatus.

facts.statement: Noasaurus is currently considered a member of the Ceratosauria.
facts.quote: Noasaurus hoy se considera miembro de la Ceratosauria.

facts.statement: Originally, Noasaurus was thought to be a member of the Coelurosauria.
facts.quote: Originalmente, fue visto como un miembro de la Coelurosauria.

facts.statement: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul classified them as members of the Abelisauridae and created the subfamily Noasaurinae.
facts.quote: En 1988, Gregory S. Paul los vio como miembros de los Abelisauridae y acuñó un Noasaurinae dentro de ese grupo.

facts.statement: Later studies recognized Noasaurids as close relatives of the larger abelisaurids.
facts.quote: Más tarde, los noasáuridos fueron reconocidos como parientes cercanos de los abelisáuridos más grandes.

facts.statement: Both Noasaurids and abelisaurids are believed to descend from the same basal abelisauroid ancestor.
facts.quote: Ambos se derivan del mismo ancestro abelisauroide basal.

facts.statement: Recent evidence supports the placement of Noasauridae within Abelisauroidea, partly because Noasaurus jaws share marked traits with abelisauroids.
facts.quote: La pertenencia de Noasauridae al grupo Abelisauroidea, ha sumado evidencia en años recientes entre otras cosas debido a que las mandíbulas de Noasaurus comparten marcados rasgos con las de los abelisauroides.
